conversation.content: Let's design a real-time chat system like WhatsApp or Slack. It needs to support 1:1 and group messaging. What clarifying questions do you have?

A few things. What's the DAU and peak concurrent connections? What's the maximum group size? Do we need message persistence, read receipts, and presence indicators? And what's our delivery guarantee — at-least-once or exactly-once?

100 million DAU, peak 20 million concurrent. Group chats up to 1,000 members. Messages must be persisted permanently. Read receipts yes, presence as a stretch goal. At-least-once with client-side deduplication is fine. Let's go.

Capacity first. 100M DAU, say 50 messages per user per day: 5 billion messages/day, about 58K messages/sec. Each message averages 200 bytes, so 1TB/day of message data. For connections: 20M concurrent WebSocket connections. A well-tuned server handles about 500K connections, so we need around 40 WebSocket gateway servers. The core architectural challenge is routing: when User A sends a message to User B, and they're on different gateway servers, how does the message get there?
Exactly. Walk me through your connection and routing architecture.

I'd design a connection gateway layer with consistent hashing of user IDs to WebSocket servers. When a user connects, their user_id is hashed to determine which gateway server they should connect to. A load balancer or DNS-based routing directs them to the right server. This means if you know the user_id, you can deterministically compute which gateway server holds their connection. No need for a centralized connection registry lookup on every message delivery — the routing is implicit in the hash function.
What happens when a gateway server goes down? The consistent hash ring maps users to a dead server.

When a gateway dies, the consistent hash ring removes that node, and the affected user IDs remap to neighboring nodes. The clients will detect the broken WebSocket and reconnect. On reconnect, the client's load balancer or service mesh routes them to the new consistent-hash-determined gateway. During the failover window — maybe 5-10 seconds — messages destined for those users can't be pushed. To handle this, I have a fallback: messages are always persisted to the database first. If the push to the gateway fails (connection not found or server unreachable), the message is stored as undelivered. When the client reconnects, it does a sync — fetching all messages since its last known sequence number. This guarantees no message loss even during gateway failures.
Let's talk about cross-server message routing. User A is on gateway 5, User B is on gateway 12. How does the message flow?

I'd use Redis pub/sub for cross-server routing. Each gateway server subscribes to a Redis channel named after its server ID — like 'gateway:12'. When gateway 5 receives a message for User B, it computes the consistent hash of User B's ID, determines gateway 12 is the target, and publishes the message to the 'gateway:12' Redis channel. Gateway 12's subscription callback receives the message and pushes it through User B's WebSocket. The advantage of Redis pub/sub over direct server-to-server gRPC is decoupling — gateways don't need to maintain connections to every other gateway. With 40 servers, that's 40 Redis subscriptions per server, not 40 bidirectional gRPC connections.
Redis pub/sub is fire-and-forget — if the subscribing gateway is temporarily disconnected from Redis, messages are lost. How do you handle that?

This is exactly why I persist messages to the database before attempting the push. Redis pub/sub is an optimization for low-latency delivery, not the source of truth. The message delivery flow is: 1) Write message to database with status 'sent'. 2) Attempt push via Redis pub/sub. 3) If the recipient's gateway acknowledges delivery, update status to 'delivered'. 4) If push fails or times out, the message stays as 'sent' in the database. The recipient's client will pick it up during its next sync. The sync happens on reconnection and also periodically — every 30 seconds the client sends a lightweight sync request with its last known sequence number. This belt-and-suspenders approach means Redis pub/sub loss is a latency degradation, not a correctness issue.
Good reliability model. How do you handle message ordering in conversations?

Each conversation has a monotonically increasing sequence number. When a message arrives at the chat service, it's assigned the next sequence number for that conversation. I'd use a Redis INCR on a key like 'seq:{conversation_id}' — atomic and fast. Even in a group chat with multiple concurrent senders, each message gets a unique, ordered sequence number. The client displays messages sorted by sequence number, not by local timestamps which could be skewed. If messages arrive out of order due to network delays, the client buffers and reorders them by sequence number before displaying.
For a group chat with 1,000 members, one message means pushing to 1,000 connections across potentially 40 gateway servers. How do you make that efficient?

I'd batch the fan-out by gateway server. Compute the consistent hash for each of the 1,000 member user IDs, group them by target gateway, and publish one message per gateway to its Redis pub/sub channel — including the list of recipient user IDs on that gateway. So instead of 1,000 individual Redis publish operations, it's at most 40 — one per gateway. Each gateway then locally multicasts to the relevant WebSocket connections. For groups with very frequent messages, I'd also consider a Kafka-backed approach where each gateway subscribes to group topics, but for our scale the batched Redis pub/sub is sufficient.
How do you store messages at scale? 1TB per day adds up fast.

I'd use Cassandra for message storage. The partition key is conversation_id, and the clustering key is the sequence number. This gives us efficient writes — append-only to a partition — and efficient reads — fetch messages in a conversation ordered by sequence number. Cassandra handles the write throughput of 58K messages/sec easily across a modest cluster. At 1TB/day, we'd accumulate 365TB/year. Cassandra's storage is cheap with commodity disks, and we can set a TTL on older messages or tier them to cold storage like S3 after, say, 2 years. For recent messages, I'd cache the last 50 messages per conversation in Redis for instant feed loading.
How do read receipts work in this architecture?

When a user reads a conversation, the client sends a read-receipt event with the conversation_id and the sequence number of the last read message. The server updates a per-user-per-conversation read pointer — stored in Redis as a hash: 'read_ptr:{conversation_id}' with field user_id and value sequence_number. For 1:1 chats, we push the read receipt to the other participant via the same Redis pub/sub routing. For group chats, we don't push every read receipt in real-time — that would be 1,000 pushes every time anyone reads. Instead, group read receipts are pulled on demand: when a user opens a message, the client queries the read pointers to show 'seen by 15 of 40 members'. This pull-vs-push distinction is key for group scalability.
We're running out of time. Any final additions?

Three things I'd add. Push notifications via APNs and FCM for users whose app is backgrounded — the gateway detects the WebSocket is closed and routes through push notification service instead. End-to-end encryption using the Signal protocol — keys exchanged out of band, server only sees ciphertext, which also means we can't moderate content server-side. And monitoring: WebSocket connection counts per gateway, message delivery latency p50/p99, Redis pub/sub lag, and Cassandra write latency.
Excellent design. The consistent hashing for connection routing and the belt-and-suspenders delivery model were particularly strong. Thanks.

strengths: Consistent hashing for deterministic connection routing eliminated the need for a centralized connection registry
Clear message delivery guarantee model — persistence first, push as optimization, sync as safety net
Excellent group chat optimization — batched fan-out by gateway and pull-based read receipts
weaknesses: Didn't explicitly define API endpoints or message format schema
Presence (online/offline) was deferred and not discussed even briefly
